webTitle: Bank of England warns of growing financial risks from ‘opaque’ AI financing – business live

fields.headline: Bank of England warns of growing financial risks from ‘opaque’ AI financing – business live
fields.standfirst: UK central bank says the very rapid expansion and broadening of funding for AI industry poses a threat to financial stability
fields.trailText: UK central bank says the very rapid expansion and broadening of funding for AI industry poses a threat to financial stability
fields.body:
1.35pm GMT

Marlboro maker Altria says considering takeover of Davidoff maker Imperial Bands

Marlboro maker Altria has just said ‌it is considering a takeover ⁠of Britain’s Imperial Brands, which makes Davidoff cigarettes and Blu vapes.

Imperial Brands shares jumped 13.1% on the news, making it the top FTSE 100 riser.

In a statement to the London stock exchange, Altria said it is exploring a potential cash offer for the Bristol-based company.

Altria Group notes the recent press speculation and confirms that it is considering a possible offer for Imperial Brands. Any offer, if made, is likely to be solely in cash.

Altria confirms it is also in discussions with a third party regarding its possible acquisition of part of the business of Imperial Brands, however no agreement has yet been reached.

Altria owns Philip Morris USA, the maker of Marlboro cigarettes, as well as the NJOY vape brand.

There was the usual cautionary statement:

There can be no certainty that an offer will ultimately be made nor as to the terms on which any offer may be made.

Earlier, Bloomberg News reported that Japan Tobacco is evaluating a potential acquisition ⁠of Imperial Brands.

The FTSE 100 company last week set out plans to cut up to 4,600 jobs in a huge cost-saving drive as it uses more AI and other technologies.

As cigarette volumes decline, the group – which is also behind the John Player Special, Golden Virginia and Rizla brands – has been revamping its business, moving towards newer products including vapes, heated tobacco and oral nicotine.

It faces tax increases in Germany and a ban on the advertising of vaping and nicotine products in the UK from next June.

Related: Tobacco group Imperial Brands to axe up to 4,600 jobs as it uses more AI

Updated at 1.41pm GMT

12.53pm GMT

European stock markets rise

European stock markets have rebounded from yesterday’s sell-off.

The FTSE 100 index in London is 1.4% ahead at 10,570, up nearly 144 points.

The Dax in Frankfurt has jumped even more, 1.9%, while the CAC 40 in Paris has gained 1.6% and the FTSE MiB in Milan has leapt by 2%.

Brent crude is 0.77% higher on the day, but is trading below $96 a barrel, at $95.34 a barrel.

Yesterday, Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said the flow of crude oil through the strait of Hormuz is approaching levels seen before the Iran war, about 80% of pre-war levels. He and other policymakers were responding to questions from MPs on the Treasury committee but he added:

But obviously it’s a pretty unpredictable.

Updated at 1.00pm GMT

12.39pm GMT

Bailey: Banks should prepare for quantum risks

Asked whether it’s even possible for banks to start preparing for quantum computing risks, Andrew Bailey said “I think it is”.

The BoE governor explained that a year ago, the Bank was very focused on quantum as the next big thing coming down the track, adding:

What has happened…is that frontier AI has come on…if you talk to the people that run the big AI companies, they were surprised by the sense of the power of these models, recursive learning of these models…and what’s happened since.”

“It’s slightly moved quantum into the background…as you can see, we are very intentionally saying we can’t forget about quantum computing, it’s still coming down the track. It could have powers that go beyond what we’re seeing with frontier AI and have substantial power to undermine cryptography.”

[concerns around quantum computing centre on the possibility that it could, in future, be used to break the public-key cryptographic encryption used to secure financial transactions].

Related: UK must learn lessons from AI race and retain its quantum computing talent, says minister

12.29pm GMT

Back to Heathrow. Ministers have “failed to make the case” for a third runway at the airport, according to a damning report by MPs.

Responding to the committee’s report, Heathrow’s chief executive, Thomas Woldbye, said the third runway still had strong support.

The overwhelming weight of evidence and support remains strongly behind Heathrow expansion. Trade unions, business groups, airlines, regional airports, senior cabinet ministers and the majority of MPs back expansion because they recognise it is vital to creating quality jobs and supporting long-term economic growth across the UK.

The case for expanding Heathrow has been examined more thoroughly than almost any infrastructure project in modern Britain…The focus now should be on delivering this privately financed project which will unlock opportunity across the country while meeting clear tests on affordability, financeability and sustainability.

The report comes a day after Heathrow released polling showing three-quarters of Labour MPs backed the expansion plan. It hopes to secure planning permission for a third runway by 2029, building it over the course of the following decade.

Despite Andy Burnham’s ambivalence, the chancellor John Healey and transport secretary Heidi Alexander have said it remains government policy, with the Conservatives and Reform both recently speaking out strongly in favour of the third runway.

But campaigners said that the report showed that Heathrow expansion should not go ahead. Friends of the Earth said continued government support for the plan “would be flying in the face of the evidence.”

Greenpeace said it would be the antithesis of Burnham’s stated aims of good growth in every postcode, “draining jobs away from the rest of the country while bringing more traffic and pollution to south west London”.

12.29pm GMT

In relation to questions on quantum computing risks, BoE governor Andrew Bailey said:

“the lifetime of these AI models is a very very small number of months. We talked about Mythos back in April - Mythos is history.”

He said the Bank was “aware” that there are now versions of these AI models coming out of production process that are causing concern among developers, who are “expressing concerns that these models got even more powerful”

“We are on the exponential part of the curve”, he added. The question is how long that will go on for? We don’t know.” That is bringing about a lot of caution about how these models are being released for the world at large, he said. “It’s important that we’re all focused on these things.”

12.29pm GMT

During today’s Bank of England press conference, Reuters asked about the Treasury Committee’s criticism earlier this year, suggesting BoE was taking a wait and see approach on AI.

Q: Do you think they were correct, they asked and in hindsight do you think you should have approached AI differently?

Andrew Bailey said that “with all due respect to the committee, I don’t think they were forseeing frontier AI. Because…if you talk to the people who run AI companies, they didn’t foresee frontier AI” or the “power of these models”, he said, adding that the Bank itself was doing a lot of work on AI internally.

Deputy governor Sarah Breeden added:

“I think what the developments in the spring highlighted to me was this point about tech surprise and the pace of development, developers were surprised, we were supriswed, maybe we should expect to be surprised in the future again. And so doing our very best to get ahead of these issues is a sensible strategy.”

Bailey said: “that is why we’ve made the point about quantum [computing risks] today.”

On quantum computing, the Bank’s financial stability report said firms need to keep pace with the growing scale and sophistication of cyber threats, including by “ensuring that any deployment of frontier AI to identify and remediate cyber threats is undertaken safely, while accelerating long-term preparations for quantum-resistant cryptography”.

12.22pm GMT

Employers: do you have concerns about the rollout of Muse and other AI agents?

Meta has rolled out its Muse AI assistant, which can be tasked with shopping, booking tickets and carrying out negotiations on a user’s behalf, across countries including the UK, US, Canada, Australia and Japan.

The AI agent needs the customer’s permission to go out and make purchases, connect to apps, use bank details or send emails autonomously. However, the possibility of employees connecting their Muse assistant to their work emails and databases is a concern for companies and their clients.

The UK Information Commissioner’s Office says firms using agentic AI “must be able to demonstrate how they comply with UK data protection law on an ongoing basis, including by identifying … steps to mitigate risks of harm to users and the wider public”.

Are you an employer or senior manager who has concerns about the rollout of Muse and similar AI assistants? Have you heard of examples of where the technology has gone wrong?

What steps are you taking to manage the problem? Are you changing guidance or issuing new advice to employees on how to deal with agentic AI?

We would love to hear from you! You can get in touch via the link below.

Related: Employers: do you have concerns about the rollout of Muse and other AI agents?

12.17pm GMT

The head of the Bank of England’s Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) has declared that the risk to financial firms from a possible artificial intelligence bubble was a “very live” issue for supervisors.

Speaking at today’s press conference in London, Katherine Braddick said:

“We have seen improvements in the quality of portfolio management, and we are in close touch with (firms) about how they’re seeing these risks change in real time.

“So it’s a very live part of what we’re doing in our supervision of the relevant firms.”

11.45am GMT

BoE's Bailey calls for international effort to test AI models

BoE governor Andrew Bailey has called for an international effort to improve the testing of artificial intelligence models – both before and after their release.

Speaking at a press conference in London today, he explained:

“We’ve got to see other countries come in, come on board with this. Whatever your view on multilateralism in different countries around the world — you probably know who I’m talking about — these are common risks.

“AI does not stop at the borders, and so we need to tackle these questions together.”

11.35am GMT

Ministers ‘fail to make case’ for Heathrow third runway, MPs report says

Ministers have “failed to make the case” for a third runway at Heathrow, according to a damning report by MPs.

The Commons transport committee said on Thursday that the detailed policy papers laid out by the government showed that expanding the London airport would fall short of pledges on the economy and climate.

The chair of the committee, Ruth Cadbury, said plans for the third runway “should be grounded” and the government needed to “go back to the drawing board”.

Heathrow is seeking to build a third runway and expand its terminals at a cost of about £33bn to almost double passenger numbers, adding up to 276,000 flights a year.

Related: Ministers ‘fail to make case’ for Heathrow third runway, MPs report says

The committee was tasked with examining the government’s Heathrow expansion national policy statement (HENPS) – but Cadbury there was a “complete disjoint” between the plans and a lack of wider aviation strategy.

The report found that the case was not made across the four tests ministers had set for expansion – that it deliver growth across the country, without harmful impacts on climate, noise and air quality.

The report said that while the government was designating the runway as a critical national project, the economic growth projections in modelling commissioned by the Department for Transport were a fraction of previous estimates – a 0.05% boost to GDP rather than o.5% – and did not justify the designation.

It said that expansion was “not currently compatible with the UK’s legally binding climate targets, and it seems impossible for the additional carbon dioxide emissions it will generate to be offset elsewhere in the economy”.

MPs said that the case for “potential compatibility rests too heavily on delivery of technologies” such as greener fuel and carbon capture which was “nowhere near the necessary trajectories”.

11.28am GMT

Bank of England warns of growing financial risks as AI borrowing jumps

The Bank of England has warned that the surge in borrowing by AI companies, and the growing sophistication of AI models, both pose a risk to the UK’s financial security.

The Bank’s Financial Policy Committee pointed to the jump in AI investment in its latest financial stability report, released this morning.

It acknowledged that this spending has supported global growth, before warning:

However, the very rapid expansion and broadening of its financing – in a form that is increasingly complex, circular and opaque – is also contributing to a deepening of interconnections across the global financial system, making it increasingly likely for stress in one area to propagate to another.

[That reference to ‘circular’ financing is a nod to the interconnected deals between AI companies; Nvidia, for example, has invested in AI companies who have then bought its own chips]

Related: Do OpenAI’s multibillion-dollar deals mean exuberance has got out of hand?

The Bank also points out that AI sector’s demand for capital is pushing up global borrowing costs, saying:

Uncertainty over the pace of data-centre development, and how much AI investment will translate into future earnings, has contributed to asset price volatility.

The Bank also noted that frontier AI capabilities have continued to grow since its latest financial stability report in July – creating a great risk of malicious cyber use:

Recent incidents have further illustrated the challenges in aligning and controlling both individual agents and multi-agent dynamics. These developments are making cyber and operational risks a more prominent threat to financial stability, and are contributing to deeper interconnections across the financial system through common technologies and providers.

Updated at 11.35am GMT

10.46am GMT

400,000 UK homeowners face £500 monthly increase in mortgage payments

More than 400,000 UK homeowners will face an eye-watering £500-per-month increase in their mortgage payments over the next two years, as rising interest rates heap extra pressure on households, the Bank of England has warned.

The Bank’s financial policy committee said today that out of the 7 million borrowers due to roll off fixed rate mortgages by December 2029, around 6.5 million would have to cough up extra funds to cover home loan payments.

Around 3.4 million borrowers would have to shoulder an increase of less than £100, while a further 2.7 million mortgage holders will have to pay £100-£500 more per month. The pain would be even greater for those borrowers coming off much lower interest rates, with about 430,000 due to see their monthly mortgage payments surge by more than £500.

These increases come after policymakers at the Bank of England hiked interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month. They have also hinted at another increase to combat inflationary pressure unleashed by the US war on Iran.

Over the next year alone, around 1 million households will see their payments rise by nearly £200 per month.

The news will put further pressure on prime minister Andy Burnham’s efforts to offset cost of living pressures, with chancellor John Healey having used his first budget to promise “breathing space” for hard-pressed consumers.

10.39am GMT

Neets fall but remain close to a million as Burnham tackles youth jobs crisis

The number of young people across the UK not in education, employment or training (Neet) fell in September but remained close to a million as Andy Burnham’s government pushes to tackle Britain’s youth jobs crisis.

As ministers prepare to make sweeping changes in response to Alan Milburn’s landmark report into young people and work, the Office for National Statistics said the number of Neets fell by 22,000 in the three months to September to stand at 959,000.

On an annual basis, the number of 16 to 24 year olds not earning or learning was 17,000 higher than a year ago. Although down from a peak of just over a million in March, the latest figure remains close to the highest level in a decade.

The prime minister last week promised to create an entirely new welfare system for young people after Milburn warned Britain risked “losing a generation of young people” without a radical change in course.

The former Tony Blair-era cabinet minister also called for a radical shake-up of employment support to guarantee young people would get help, alongside changes to education policy and healthcare.

It comes as a parallel review into disability benefits by the Labour minister Stephen Timms this week called for major changes to a welfare system that was “no longer fit for purpose”.

Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, said young people

deserve better. That’s why we’re fundamentally reforming how we support young people to grow up in this country.

As part of our response to the Milburn Review, we’re building a new settlement that invests in young people’s success instead of paying for failure.

It is understood the government is preparing a full response to Milburn’s recommendations spelling out the changes that will be taken forward. Ministers will then publish a white paper next year on welfare reform.

Overhauling welfare will however stand as one of the biggest challenges for Burnham’s government as he pushes to curb a rising welfare bill without triggering a repeat of the backbench rebellion faced by Keir Starmer.

Updated at 10.40am GMT

9.48am GMT

Norse Atlantic Airways suspends flights as it teeters on brink of bankruptcy

Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights and said it will file for bankruptcy if it cannot secure short-term financing urgently.

The Norwegian airline, which operates long-haul flights around the world including from London Gatwick and the US to Europe and Asia, announced it was on the brink on Thursday morning, a day after warning that its finances were “critical”.

The airline, like many worldwide, is reeling from surging jet fuel prices which have sent costs skywards since the attack on Iran in February, as well as hitting consumer confidence.

In a statement to the Oslo stock exchange, Norse said:

If a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently, it is the Board’s ​intention to file for bankruptcy.

It said it was still looking at options to secure short-term financing and was in discussion with investors regarding a possible takeover, but warned:

There can be no assurance that a viable solution will ​be found.

Norse was founded in 2021 as it sought to step into the space vacated by Norwegian Air, whose attempts to fly budget long-haul were also abandoned as unviable.

Despite that, Norse revived the transatlantic routes, with a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 Dreamliners and ​many former Norwegian staff.

Norse said in the summer it was exploring a potential sale or merger, and set out on a cost-cutting programme called Project Falcon to save $50 million, including axing around 75 jobs. It also moved its headquarters out of Norway to cheaper offices in Latvia, while the founder and chief executive, Bjorn Tore Larsen, left the airline.

It said it “sincerely apologises to its passengers for the inconvenience caused by this situation”.

UK flights affected include London Gatwick to Orlando, Bangkok and Cape Town. A winter service from Manchester to Thailand was due to start operating next month.

9.27am GMT

‘It’s in quite a dark place’: why UK housebuilding is struggling

A shopping centre in London that was due to be knocked down and replaced with a retail emporium and more than 1,000 apartments has been paused, dealing another blow to the government’s housing targets.

Lewisham council’s Green administration, which swept into power in May, insisted a larger number of affordable homes should be included in plans agreed last year with Labour officials.

Landsec, which owns the 1980s red-brick shopping centre in the borough’s town centre, said last month that the council’s demand, combined with “exceptionally challenging economic conditions”, had forced a rethink.

For London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, the lack of progress in the capital’s south-east corner raises alarm bells as he tries to lift homebuilding across the city.

Related: ‘It’s in quite a dark place’: why UK housebuilding is struggling

According to Damien Sharkey, the managing director of Hub, a mid-sized UK urban property developer with much of its work in London, the outlook for 2027 is “one of the most challenging in the firm’s 15-year history”.

After a collapse in housing starts to just 4,100 across London in 2025, figures have improved, with 16,290 homes registered in the year to the end of June 2026.

However, this impressive 298% year-on-year growth spurt only takes the capital back to where it was in 2023-24, and well below the 21,660 starts in 2022-23.

Khan’s efforts are not helped by a building safety levy on developers, expected to raise £3.4bn over 10 years, combined with extra regulations governing how to build and insulate tower blocks after the 2017 Grenfell Tower disaster.

9.22am GMT

The AI doomsday threat: Distinguishing facts from fear

On the AI front, The Guardian is running a livestreamed event next Monday, entitled: The AI doomsday threat: Distinguishing facts from fear.

On Monday 30 November, join Dan Milmo, the Guardian’s global technology editor; Professor Dame Wendy Hall, Regius professor of computer science at the University of Southampton; Stuart J. Russell, a British computer scientist known for his contributions to AI and professor of computer science at the University of California, Berkeley; and Alexandra Birch-Mayne, personal chair of multilingual natural language prrocessing in the School of Informatics at the University of Edinburgh.

They will discuss the warnings surrounding artificial intelligence and how we can separate fact from speculation. Livestreamed only.

Recent claims from AI researchers have brought concerns about superintelligence into mainstream political debate. But how credible are these apocalyptic predictions? Are AI companies genuinely losing control of the technology? Or are these distracting us from harms already unfolding, including misinformation, cybercrime, job displacement and the concentration of corporate power?

Book tickets here or at guardian.live.

Updated at 9.24am GMT

9.15am GMT

London commuters braced for disruption as tube strike begins

Severe disruption is expected across the London Underground today and tomorrow, when many tube drivers will go on strike.

Drivers who are part of the national union of rail, maritime and transport workers (RMT) will strike for 24 hours from noon on Thursday, in the first of a fresh wave of strikes in the long-running dispute over the planned introduction of a four-day working week.

Talks to avert the strike ended at the Acas conciliation service on Tuesday without resolution.

The RMT has planned seven more strike dates, including two 24-hour stoppages in the week before Christmas, which will affect transport during four of the busiest shopping days in the capital.

Related: London commuters braced for disruption as tube strike begins

The union, which represents just under half of tube drivers, claimed that the changes to working patterns were being imposed and could lead to increased fatigue and affect safety.

London Underground said the changes were voluntary, and the strike has been described as “strange” by the rival drivers’ union. Aslef, a union representing a slight majority of Tube drivers, warmly welcomed the proposal for a shorter working week.

Transport for London (TfL) warned passengers to plan ahead and expect disruption on all lines. Most tube lines will continue to operate today, aside from the Piccadilly and Circle lines. The Waterloo & City line will be closed from midday.

Reduced services are expected across the rest of the tube network from late morning and will finish earlier in the evening. No service is expected after 9pm.

On Friday, trains will start running later than usual, from about 7am, and remain disrupted through the afternoon, with normal services only expected to resume by early evening.

The Elizabeth line, London Overground and national rail services will run as usual, but are expected to be crowded. Buses are not directly affected, but are likely to be busier than usual and slowed by increased congestion on the roads.

9.08am GMT

No evidence China orchestrated Nvidia CEO's affair, officials brief Congress – WSJ

There was no evidence a Chinese tech executive who had an affair with Nvidia boss Jensen Huang was directed by Chinese intelligence to spy on him, US officials told congressional staffers in a highly classified briefing on Tuesday, according to the Wall Street Journal.

The current evidence collected by the US suggests Alice Huang and the Nvidia CEO’s relationship may have been amorous, not a coordinated play by China in the race for advanced chips, the newspaper said. New information could change that, though.

The briefers said that the ministry of state security (MSS), China’s premier spy agency, approached Alice Huang to provide it with information, as compelled under Chinese law. She was in contact with the spy agency during the affair, they said. But the US does not have any indications she disclosed intelligence of significance to the MSS.

The discussion with congressional staffers, which was a broad overview rather than a detailed intelligence rundown, occurred a day after Jensen Huang was reinstalled as CEO following Donald Trump’s intervention. The US president assured Nvidia that Huang posed no national security threat.

Trump and JD Vance, the vice president, intervened in Nvidia’s leadership drama and put pressure on the tech company’s board to reinstall Huang as the CEO despite other lawmakers’ concerns over whether Huang posed a national security risk for having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Huang had stepped down following reports that the board was preparing to oust him and that he had other affairs, including one with an Nvidia executive.

The CEO’s allies have said that there is not enough evidence proving Alice Huang is a spy or that Nvidia knew about alleged efforts to smuggle chips to China. Some current and former US officials have said that regardless of what information changed hands, the fact that one of America’s most influential businesspeople had an affair with a woman connected to Chinese intelligence posed national security risks.

Huang apologised to staff on Tuesday for the tumult he caused at Nvidia.

Related: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologizes to staff: ‘I made some terrible mistakes’

8.55am GMT

Britain signs £8.7bn submarine contract with Babcock to ensure it's 'warfighting ready'

Britain has signed an £8.7bn contract ⁠to upgrade its nuclear submarine facilities with the defence contractor Babcock today, as part of efforts to ensure the country is “warfighting ready“.

Citing the growing ⁠threat from Russia, Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said last month that Britain needs to be ⁠ready to fight or deter military action within 1,000 ​days. He said today:

Our nuclear submarines ‌are the cornerstone of our national security.

Even when we have to move funding from other departments, we will prioritise our nuclear deterrent and getting Britain warfighting ready.

The ​deal – Babcock’s biggest ever contract – will create around 3,000 new ​highly skilled ‌jobs, mainly across ​Plymouth, Clyde ​and Bristol, as well as 2,500 apprentice and graduate roles over five years. It will also will safeguard 8,500 existing nuclear defence jobs at Babcock.

It brings together critical submarine maintenance, engineering, naval base and enabling services.

Babcock is the biggest riser on the FTSE 100 index this morning, up 5.7%.

The ‌five-year contract, which could run up to 15 years, will be the single biggest procurement decision of the current ​parliament, Streeting said, and will ensure submarine maintenance can be done more quickly.

In recent years, Royal Navy submarines, which ensure Britain’s continuous at sea deterrence policy, have ⁠had to conduct longer than usual deployments because ​of a ​lack of maintenance facilities.

Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said:

With this new agreement we’re not just investing in our national security, we’re also making a huge investment in our people. We’re providing opportunities to get young people into work, to bring jobs to communities in Plymouth, Clyde and beyond, and to boost growth across the UK.

Updated at 9.11am GMT

8.29am GMT

FCA admits miscalculating part of car finance compensation

Britain’s financial regulator has admitted that it has miscalculated part of the compensation scheme for victims of the car finance scandal, and told Barclays to stop making settlement offers while it works through the data issues.

In March, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) announced a £9.1bn compensation scheme for drivers were overcharged for loans as a result of commission payments between lenders and car dealers.

However, it is embroiled in an ongoing legal battle which has forced the regulator to partly suspend the scheme, and a hearing to decide what happens is due to go ahead in February next year.

On Thursday, the FCA said that it had identified “some errors in how we categorised a small group of loan agreements”.

While the potential impact on average compensation is small - less than £10 per agreement, on average - we recognise this affects ongoing litigation.

We are sorry for the further uncertainty this creates for consumers and firms. We will provide an update on any further material developments.

Earlier this month Barclays, which has set aside £430m in connection with alleged motor finance mis-selling, started offering compensation settlements.

Barclays is the first big UK lender to begin offering payouts to some customers who have complained, with hopes the move might see some receive payments by Christmas. the FCA said:

Barclays has been offering full and final settlement offers to their customers. We have asked that they pause making these offers while we work through the data issues identified and implications they might have, if any.

Updated at 9.10am GMT

8.25am GMT

Sarah Cardell, chief executive of the CMA, said:

Millions of people across the UK rely on private dentistry as an essential service, but the market isn’t working well for them. People can’t easily compare and switch between providers, dentists are in short supply, commercial incentives to grow revenues may not operate in the patients’ best interests and there are weaknesses in the regulatory framework. As a result, many people are struggling with affordability, and those on lower incomes and in certain parts of the UK are hardest hit.

We’re proposing a wide-ranging package of measures to change the way the market operates and will work with governments across the UK to finalise these recommendations ahead of our final report in March.

The competition watchdog is developing recommendations that would:

  • Make it easier to compare and switch, through clearer treatment plans, better access to dental records and diagnostic information, and a new online source of information about NHS and private dentistry

  • Increase workforce capacity, including expanded domestic training, fuller use of dental therapists and hygienists, and fewer barriers for overseas-qualified professionals

  • Strengthen consumer protection and redress, with clearer accountability for decisions at practice or business level and better complaints and redress arrangements

  • Enable governments to more directly shape this market using their significant NHS buying power and strategic leverage to encourage more affordable private prices for essential dental care

8.14am GMT

Dental care is the medical treatment Brits are most likely to put off because of high costs, a separate report found this week – forcing some people to do their own dentristy.

Drawing on what people wrote about their care in UK forum threads, a new study by the private clinic Zental Dental set out to find which treatments people delay when they cannot cover the cost, and the dentist came up more than any other treatment.

  • Dental care is the medical treatment Brits most often delay or skip for financial reasons, with dental prices up 29% since 2021.

  • Glasses were in second place. Prices for glasses and contact lenses climbed 21% from September 2021 to September 2026. A pair of varifocals can cost as much as £500.

  • Switching to a cheaper option rather than going without is most common with prescriptions, a step 39 of 65 people took.

The research examined 16 medical treatments to find which ones people in the UK most often delay over cost. The report read 7,589 posts in 54 UK forum threads, counting how many people, per 100 describing their own experience of a treatment, had put it off, cut down, or gone without.

It measured how often each treatment was named, unprompted, in cost-of-living threads, and tracked its price rise from 2021 to 2026. The two delay measures were combined into one score out of 100, showing which treatments people put on hold most when budgets are tight.

Dental care ranks first among the medical treatments Brits delay or go without over the price. Out of every 100 people posting about their dental care, 14 said the price had led them to put treatment off, cut back or go without. Going less often or stopping altogether was the most common response, ahead of saying they could not afford a visit.

When people listed the cutbacks they had made to cope with the cost of living, 76 named dental care without being asked about their health. Dental prices rose 29% over the five years to September 2026, and a private check-up now costs £55. Some people described doing their own dentistry instead, from temporary filling kits to pulling teeth.

Updated at 8.15am GMT

7.58am GMT

UK competition watchdog calls for shake-up of £8bn dentistry market

Here is our full take:

The UK’s competition watchdog has called for a shake-up of the £8bn private dentistry market, after an investigation identified a “catalogue of concerns” including inflation-busting annual rises and evidence of targets to sell more expensive treatments and dental payment plans.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said patients faced substantial differences in prices in different parts of the UK and “commercial practices, targets and incentives [that] may not operate in patients’ best interests”.

The report said dentists typically have a financial stake in treatment revenues, either as practice owners or through revenue-sharing arrangements.

“We have also seen evidence of targets to convert NHS patients to private care, sell more expensive treatments, and increase sales of dental payment plans,” the CMA said. “Together, these incentives and practices create a risk that patients are sold treatments that are not in their best interests.”

The interim report found that prices rose by an estimated 7% a year on average between 2023 and 2025 at large dental groups, well ahead of inflation and wage growth, with costs across the industry leading some people to delay or go without treatment.

The CMA gave the example of a composite white filling that costs about 36% of mean weekly disposable income in the north-east of England and 35% in Wales.

It also identified significant price differences, even in the same local area.

In Preston, prices advertised online for a composite filling ranges from £80 to £223, while in Caerphilly the price of an amalgam filling ranged from £72 to £159. The report said:

Some variation is to be expected, but the CMA is concerned that people are paying more than they should because they are unable to shop around.

The CMA said that about 60% of patients across the UK now pay for at least some private dental care, including many on low incomes, but that it is difficult for patients to “confidently shop around and get a good deal”.

The report found that one in six private dental practices in the UK does not publish price lists online and that there was “substantial variation in indicative profit margins between dental practices”.

Another concern identified was data that suggested that practices primarily serving NHS patients do not necessarily earn lower profit margins.

7.36am GMT

Introduction: Nvidia reportedly halts chip shipments to south-east Asia as stock sell-off eases

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.

Nvidia has halted chip shipments to south-east Asia, as the sell-off in stock markets eased.

The US chipmaker, which is at the heart of the AI boom, has told manufacturing partners such as Dell and Supermicro to stop shipping servers to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, according to the Financial Times, citing three unnamed sources.

It is unclear whether this is a temporary halt. Washington has increased export controls to prevent Chinese access to AI computing power.

Some calm returned to Asian markets, after sharp declines on Wednesday. South Korea’s Kospi rose 0.45%, a day after its 7.05% tumble. Japan’s Nikkei gained 0.86%, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng climbed 1.6% and China’s CSI 300 was flat.

Beijing has issued a measured response to Donald Trump’s latest proposed US tariffs, saying China and the US should resolve their trade issues through talks, based on equality, mutual respect and reciprocity.

Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters at a briefing:

The so-called overcapacity is a false premise, and China opposes it being used as a pretext for political manipulation.

The US president is proposing new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the European Union, that would go into effect early next year, the office of the US trade representative said on Wednesday.

The administration is proposing an additional 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total tax to about 40%.

Related: Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU

In the UK, the competition watchdog has found that millions of people can’t afford private dental care, with prices rising by an inflation-busting 7% a year.

Cost is leading some people to delay or go without treatment altogether, the Competition and Markets Authority said. At large dental groups, prices rose by an estimated 7% a year on average between 2023 and 2025, ahead of inflation and wage growth.

This is particularly acute in certain regions: A composite white filling makes up around 36% of mean weekly disposable income in the North East of England and 35% in Wales.

It is hard for patients to make informed choices: it is difficult for them to confidently shop around and get a good deal, and quality is difficult to assess.

Prices can vary hugely in the same area. In Preston, prices advertised online for a composite filling ranged from £80 to £223 and in Caerphilly amalgam filling prices ranged from £72 to £159.

There is also shortage of dentists. The estimated vacancy rate for general dentists in England is around 8%, significantly higher than the 2% vacancy rate across the UK economy. The UK also has fewer dentists per head than most European countries.

webTitle: 430,000 UK homeowners face £500-plus jump in monthly mortgage payments

fields.headline: 430,000 UK homeowners face £500-plus jump in monthly mortgage payments
fields.standfirst:
Bank of England warns of increases for millions coming off fixed deals over next three years as interest rates rise

  • Business live – latest updates
fields.trailText: Bank of England warns of increases for millions coming off fixed deals over next three years as interest rates rise
fields.body:
More than 400,000 UK homeowners will face a £500-a-month increase in their mortgage payments over the next three years, as rising interest rates heap extra pressure on households, the Bank of England has said.

The Bank’s financial policy committee said on Thursday that out of the 7 million borrowers coming off fixed-rate deals before December 2029, about 6.5 million would have to cough up extra funds to cover their home loan payments.

For about 3.4 million borrowers the monthly increase would be less than £100, while for a further 2.7 million it would be £100-£500. The increase would be even greater for those borrowers coming off much lower interest rates, with about 430,000 likely to see their monthly mortgage payments surge by more than £500.

Warnings about the increases came after policymakers at the Bank of England hiked interest rates from 3.75% to 4% this month. The Bank also hinted at another increase in interest rates to combat inflationary pressure caused by the Iran war. The financial markets have predicted three quarter-point rate rises by summer 2027.

Over the next year, about 1 million households will see their payments rise by almost £200 a month.

The news will put further pressure on Andy Burnham’s efforts to offset cost of living pressures, with the chancellor, John Healey, having used his first budget to promise “breathing space” for hard-pressed consumers.

The figures came a day after the energy regulator for Great Britain raised the cap on household energy bills by 26%.

The Bank of England on Thursday also raised further concerns about cybersecurity and AI threats, recent outages at Google and Microsoft that had laid bare businesses’ growing dependence on outside technology, and how “disruption at a single provider” could “affect many firms at once”.

The financial policy committee also flagged concerns about emerging quantum computing technologies potentially undermining the crypto technology that protected essential financial transactions.

It said the evolving risks reinforced the need for “significant and sustained investment by the financial sector in building resilience”, adding that banks needed to have credible arrangements to ensure they could bounce back quickly from any disruption and maintain “vital financial services”.

The committee acknowledged this would place competing demands on lenders’ tech experts and management teams, but added that a failure to take action would “compromise firms’ operational resilience with potential system-wide implications”.

The Bank on Thursday also announced plans to further reduce capital requirements for UK banks, as part of a wider package that it said could unleash an extra £175bn in lending capacity. However, extra funding could end up being used to payout shareholders and investors.

webTitle: Ministry of Defence signs £8.7bn deal with Babcock to maintain submarines

fields.headline: Ministry of Defence signs £8.7bn deal with Babcock to maintain submarines
fields.standfirst:
Wes Streeting says deal will ‘get our subs out of the docks and into the sea faster’ amid scrutiny of nuclear deterrent

  • UK politics live – latest updates

  • Business live – latest updates
fields.trailText: Wes Streeting says deal will ‘get our subs out of the docks and into the sea faster’ amid scrutiny of nuclear deterrent
fields.body:
The Ministry of Defence has signed an £8.7bn contract with the defence company Babcock to maintain Britain’s submarine fleet amid scrutiny of the performance of the country’s nuclear deterrent.

The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said the five-year contract would “get our subs out of the docks and into the sea faster”.

The UK’s four nuclear-armed submarines patrol the oceans to provide a continuous at-sea deterrent, staying submerged to avoid detection and to be able to launch Trident missiles even if land-based weapons are destroyed.

However, even as the perceived threats to the UK have increased in recent years, particularly from Russia in the northern Atlantic, the fleet has faced concerns over its readiness after a series of faults forced some of the submarines into dry docks for months at a time.

That has forced the working subs and their crew to spend longer periods under the water. HMS Vengeance recently spent a record 217 days submerged before returning to dock this month.

The head of the Royal Navy, Gen Sir Gwyn Jenkins, said this month that the UK needed to “improve our submarine maintenance”. On the other hand, some politicians including the Green party are opposed to spending on Trident, arguing that the programme should be dismantled and the money used for other priorities.

The new contract will cover work at naval bases at Devonport in Plymouth and Faslane in Scotland, and could be extended to as long as 15 years under a separate memorandum of understanding. Babcock is also building five Type 31 frigates for the Royal Navy in Rosyth, Scotland, although it has faced cost problems.

The government said the submarine contract would create 3,000 new British jobs, plus about 2,500 apprentice and graduate opportunities.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “Keeping the public safe will always be my top priority. This investment is a clear demonstration of that commitment – supporting not just the submarines that maintain our nuclear deterrent but also the people who build and maintain them.”

Streeting said: “We’re not going to repeat the mistakes of the past, where investment in our nuclear capability was delayed. Even when we have to move funding from other departments, we will prioritise our nuclear deterrent and getting Britain war-fighting ready.”

The contract is the largest in Babcock’s history and was welcomed by investors. The FTSE 100 company’s share price was up 7% on Thursday to nearly £11 a share, the highest since August, although well below its record peak of nearly £15 earlier in the year.

Harry Holt was promoted from leading Babcock’s nuclear division to chief executive in July, after his predecessor’s retirement. Holt said the deal would “increase submarine availability and develop the skills, infrastructure and capability to support the Royal Navy’s submarine force for the years ahead.”

webTitle: Norse Atlantic Airways suspends all flights as it makes urgent funding plea

fields.headline: Norse Atlantic Airways suspends all flights as it makes urgent funding plea
fields.standfirst:
Norwegian airline says its finances are ‘critical’ and it will file for bankruptcy if it cannot secure short-term backing

  • Business live – latest updates
fields.trailText: Norwegian airline says its finances are ‘critical’ and it will file for bankruptcy if it cannot secure short-term backing
fields.body:
Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights and said it will file for bankruptcy if it cannot secure short-term financing urgently.

The Norwegian airline, which operates long-haul flights around the world including from London Gatwick and the US to Europe and Asia, announced it was on the brink on Thursday morning, a day after warning that its finances were “critical”.

The airline, like many worldwide, is reeling from surging jet fuel prices that have sent costs skywards since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February, as well as hitting consumer confidence.

In a statement to the Oslo stock exchange, Norse said: “If a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently, it is the board’s ​intention to file for bankruptcy.”

It said it was still looking at options to secure short-term financing and was in discussion with investors regarding a possible takeover but said: “There can be no assurance that a viable solution will ​be found.”

Norse was founded in 2021 as it sought to step into the space vacated by Norwegian Air, whose attempts to fly budget long-haul were also abandoned as unviable.

Despite that, Norse revived the transatlantic routes, with a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 Dreamliners and ​many former Norwegian staff.

Norse said in the summer it was exploring a potential sale or merger, and set out on a cost-cutting programme called Project Falcon to save $50m (£38m), including axing about 75 jobs. It also moved its headquarters out of Norway to cheaper offices in Latvia, while the founder and chief executive, Bjørn Tore Larsen, left the airline.

It said it “sincerely apologises to its passengers for the inconvenience caused by this situation”.

UK routes affected include London Gatwick to Orlando, Bangkok and Cape Town. A winter service from Manchester to Thailand was due to start operating next month.

webTitle: A vocal cohort of tech leaders celebrates Huang’s Nvidia return, but others are keeping quiet

fields.headline: A vocal cohort of tech leaders celebrates Huang’s Nvidia return, but others are keeping quiet
fields.standfirst: Elon Musk and Sam Altman among those rejoicing but Google, Meta and Apple chiefs have declined to weigh in
fields.trailText: Elon Musk and Sam Altman among those rejoicing but Google, Meta and Apple chiefs have declined to weigh in
fields.body:
The phrase “return of the king” rippled across social media on Monday. A vocal subsection of the tech industry was celebrating the resurrection of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. Some called him the “imperial and royal majesty”, others anointed him as “our Jesus” and several simply posted a crown emoji.

“The mistake has been corrected,” said Elon Musk. “Jensen!” exclaimed OpenAI’s Sam Altman.

It had been a whirlwind two weeks that started with the ouster of Huang as Nvidia’s CEO after his admission of an extramarital affair with a woman some in the US government feared to be a Chinese spy. Two more alleged affairs with company employees were later revealed. Silicon Valley engineers and venture capitalists decried Huang’s departure at the time, writing an open letter to Nvidia’s board of directors saying: “Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice.”

Donald Trump also got involved. The president repeatedly said that he’d like to see the return of Huang calling the CEO a “fine person” and “honorable guy”.

In the meantime, Nvidia’s stock tanked, falling more than 10%, and shedding hundreds of billions in value. Nvidia, which designs powerful computing chips used for artificial intelligence, is among the world’s top five most valuable companies.

On Monday, in a stunning reversal, Nvidia’s board unanimously voted to reinstate Huang. The decision came after Trump dialed into the company’s Sunday board meeting to advocate for Huang’s return. In a statement, the White House said: “We have to protect our geniuses.”

Nvidia’s stock rebounded, gaining nearly $1tn in market value. Trump, who owns shares in the chip maker, took a victory lap, making up to $15m with the surge on Monday.

Silicon Valley’s venture capitalists also rejoiced. Jason Calacanis, an angel investor, Nvidia stock-holder and co-host of the tech-centric All-In podcast, wrote a flurry of posts on X. He posted an AI image of a shining long-haired Huang depicted as Jesus holding a graphics processing unit (GPU) in place of the bible, writing: “GPU Jesus has risen.”

Other tech figures took the news personally. Travis Kalanick, the disgraced Uber CEO who was pushed out by his board, was one of the top figures fighting for Huang’s reinstatement. In past weeks, he frequently posted on X, saying “Bring Jensen back”, “LFG” (Let’s fucking go), and “We’ve got your back”.

Kalanick was reportedly among a small group of venture capitalists who lobbied Trump and JD Vance to push Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang, according to the FT. On Monday, Kalanick posted: “I will always sign up to serve him.”

‘We’re all being gaslit’

While a vocal cohort of Silicon Valley insiders high-fived Huang’s return, it’s been radio silence from several other of the industry’s top leaders and rank-and-file workers.

The CEOs of Google, Meta and Apple have not weighed in on the debate. When Amazon’s Jeff Bezos was asked at an event last week if he thought Huang should be reinstated, he responded: “I don’t know enough of the details … so I can’t answer that question.” Microsoft’s Satya Nadella had a similar response.

Anil Dash, an entrepreneur with a career in leading smaller tech companies, is one of the few voices in tech who has publicly criticized Huang’s reinstatement. He says it sends the wrong message to the industry – that there are no rules, boundaries or accountability.

Dash pointed to widespread rationale for Huang’s return, which is based on the CEO being singularly crucial in the AI arms race against China. Calacanis, for example, has trumpeted this justification, saying: “We can not [sic] lose the race for super intelligence to China – period, full stop.”

And now, Dash said, Huang could have been compromised by a Chinese asset, and he’s running the biggest company in the industry. “It doesn’t make any sense,” he said. “We’re all being gaslit and we’re at a certain point where we’re like, ‘No, the sky’s not green. The sky’s blue.’”

Dash says the hundreds of thousands of tech workers who live in fear of being swept up in the increasingly frequent waves of layoffs, as the industry pivots to AI, aren’t able to speak up even if they disagree with Huang’s reinstatement. They don’t know if their “boss agrees with these guys”, Dash said.

Alison Taylor, an associate professor at New York University’s Stern Business School, said that mentality extends beyond Silicon Valley to the White House, given that Trump played a part in Huang’s return. “Trump’s whole thing is retaliation,” she noted.

“The message is: if you don’t shut up and go along with it, you’re not going to survive,” Taylor said. “It’s a fuck you to everybody who believes in the rule of law and who believes in anything being fair.”

Huang apologized to Nvidia staff in a company-wide meeting on Tuesday for “some terrible mistakes” he made. The CEO also rejected narratives that he was a “tech bro” who was “above the law”, adding it was “completely untrue” that Trump pressured Nvidia’s board to reinstate him.

“Everything he’s done, it’s just his affection, his admiration, his recognition of the great company that you are,” Huang said of Trump.

In a separate statement, Huang thanked leaders across the industry for their “extraordinary support”.

“I can’t wait to get back to work,” he added.
